column8: Exactly one living person: Abraham, an old man. Sarah's body lies covered from head to foot by a plain cloth, her face hidden. No servants, mourners or children.
column9: Inside a tent at Hebron in the land of Canaan, its front open to the hills, Abraham sits on the ground in mourning before the body of Sarah his wife. Her body lies on a mat, covered from head to foot with a plain cloth, and Abraham weeps for her with his head bowed in the soft, muted light.

column4: Abraham asks for a burying place
column8: Abraham is the only one of his household; all the others are the sons of Heth, grown men of the city. No women or children, and no graves or tombs in view.
column9: At the gate of the city of Hebron, Abraham, an old man in mourning, stands up and bows himself to the people of the land, the sons of Heth, who are gathered about the gateway. He asks them for a burying place for his dead, and they answer him with respect, calling him a mighty prince among them.

column8: Abraham is the only one of his household; the rest are men of the city. The silver is in pieces weighed on a balance, not coins. No women or children.
column9: At the gate of Hebron, in the hearing of the sons of Heth and all who go in at the gate, Abraham weighs out silver on a balance for Ephron the Hittite, a man of the city in a long robe who stands facing him. Pieces of silver lie heaped on a cloth beside the balance, and the men of the city stand around as witnesses.

column8: Exactly one person: Abraham. No servants, mourners, procession or bier. A natural cave in the rock, with no building over it.
column9: In the field of Machpelah before Mamre, with trees growing along all its borders, Abraham stands alone in grief before the dark mouth of the cave at the end of the field, where he has buried Sarah his wife. The cave opens in a low rocky bank, and the quiet field lies around him in soft light.

column8: Exactly two people: Abraham, very old, and his servant. No one else; only tents and grazing flocks in the distance.
column9: Before his tents, Abraham, old and well stricken in age, sits on a seat while Abraham's servant, the eldest servant of his house, kneels before him and puts his hand under Abraham's thigh, swearing to take a wife for Isaac from Abraham's own kindred. Flocks and herds graze in the distance, for the LORD has blessed Abraham in all things.

column8: Exactly ten camels, all kneeling. The women of the city are only far off, coming out with pitchers on their shoulders.
column9: At the time of evening, outside the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia, Abraham's servant has made his ten laden camels kneel down by a well of water, and the servant's men rest beside them. The servant stands by the well with his head bowed, praying in his heart for good speed, while far off the women of the city come out with pitchers to draw water.

column5: Rebekah, Abraham's servant, the servant's men
column8: Exactly ten camels. Rebekah alone draws the water, with one pitcher; no one helps her.
column9: In the evening by the well outside the city of Nahor, Rebekah, very fair to look upon, empties her pitcher into the trough where the ten camels drink, ready to hurry down to the well again to draw more. Abraham's servant stands a little apart, watching her in silent wonder, and the servant's men wait beside the camels.

column5: Abraham's servant, Rebekah, the servant's men
column8: Exactly ten camels, resting. Rebekah wears two gold bracelets and one golden earring. The servant bows his head where he stands, not lying on the ground.
column9: In the evening by the well, the ten camels have done drinking, and Rebekah stands wearing the golden earring upon her face and the two gold bracelets on her hands that Abraham's servant has given her. The servant bows down his head and worships the LORD, who has led him to the house of his master's kin, while the servant's men stand by the camels.

column5: Laban, Abraham's servant, the servant's men
column8: Exactly ten camels. Only Laban, the servant and the servant's men; no household servants and no women.
column9: In the evening at the house of Rebekah's family in the city of Nahor, Laban, who ran out to the well and called him in as one blessed of the LORD, welcomes Abraham's servant. The ten camels have been ungirded and are eating straw and provender, and water has been set out for the servant and the servant's men to wash their feet.

column5: Abraham's servant, Laban, the servant's men
column8: Only men: the servant, his men, Laban and Laban's father Bethuel. No women. The food before the servant is untouched.
column9: In the evening, in the lamplit house of Rebekah's family, food has been set before Abraham's servant, but he will not eat until he has told his errand. He sits before the untouched food and speaks earnestly of his master Abraham and of the damsel at the well, while Laban and his father Bethuel, an older man, listen, and the servant's men sit behind him.

column5: Abraham's servant, Rebekah, Laban, Rebekah's mother
column8: Exactly four people: the servant, Rebekah, Laban and Rebekah's mother. No household, guests or servants.
column9: By lamplight in the house of Rebekah's family, Abraham's servant brings forth jewels of silver, jewels of gold and raiment and gives them to Rebekah, who receives them quietly. He has also given precious things to Laban, her brother, and to Rebekah's mother, who stand beside her holding his gifts.

column5: Rebekah, Laban, Rebekah's mother, Abraham's servant, the servant's men
column8: Exactly ten camels. Only Rebekah, Laban, Rebekah's mother, the servant and his men; no other household or neighbours.
column9: In the morning outside the house of Rebekah's family, Abraham's servant asks to be sent away to his master, and the servant's men stand ready with the ten camels. Laban and Rebekah's mother, who wanted her to stay at least ten days, have called Rebekah to ask her, and she stands before them and answers that she will go.

column5: Rebekah, Rebekah's nurse, Rebekah's damsels, Abraham's servant, the servant's men, Laban, Rebekah's mother
column8: Exactly ten camels. Rebekah and her damsels ride on them, her nurse goes with them, and the servant leads. Only Laban and her mother see them off.
column9: In the morning outside the city of Nahor, Laban blesses his sister Rebekah as she sets out, and Rebekah's mother stands beside him. Rebekah and Rebekah's damsels ride on the camels with Rebekah's nurse, and Abraham's servant leads the way with the servant's men, out across the open country toward the land of Canaan.

column5: Isaac, Rebekah, Abraham's servant, Rebekah's nurse, Rebekah's damsels, the servant's men
column8: Exactly ten camels. Isaac, a man of forty, walks alone in the field, some way from the camels. Evening light.
column9: At eventide in a field in the south country, Isaac, a man of forty, walks alone, meditating, and lifts his eyes to see the ten camels coming. Rebekah has alighted from her camel and, told by Abraham's servant beside her that this is his master, covers herself with a veil, while Rebekah's nurse, Rebekah's damsels and the servant's men wait with the camels.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac and Rebekah. No wedding crowd, feast or servants.
column9: At dusk in the south country, Isaac brings Rebekah, still veiled, to the door of his mother Sarah's tent among his tents. He takes her to be his wife and loves her, and his face, long sad for his mother's death, is comforted as he looks at her.

column8: Exactly seven people: Abraham and Keturah's six sons. No women, children, flocks or crowd.
column9: Before his tents, Abraham, now very old, stands watching as the six sons of Keturah set out eastward to the east country, with the gifts he has given them loaded on their pack animals. The six walk away from him across the open land toward the morning sun rising in the east.

column8: Exactly one person: Abraham, very old, lying at rest. No mourners, sons or servants.
column9: Inside his tent, its front open to the quiet land, Abraham lies at rest on his bed, a very old man full of years, with his eyes closed and his face at peace. He has died in a good old age, at the end of a life of a hundred and seventy-five years.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac and Ishmael, both grown men, Ishmael fourteen years the elder. No servants, procession or bier.
column9: In the field of Ephron before Mamre, with trees along its borders, Abraham's sons Isaac and Ishmael (old) stand side by side in mourning before the dark mouth of the cave of Machpelah at the end of the field, where they have buried their father beside Sarah. Isaac is a bearded man of seventy-five, and Ishmael, fourteen years older, is grey-bearded.

column8: Exactly thirteen people: Ishmael, very old, and his twelve sons, all grown men. No women, children or crowd.
column9: In the desert country between Havilah and Shur, Ishmael (old) sits before his tent with his twelve sons standing around him, the twelve princes of their nations, grown men in desert robes. Beyond them stand their towns and strongholds among the desert hills, where his people dwell.

column8: Exactly one person: Rebekah, with child, a woman many years married. God is only radiant light from above, no figure or face.
column9: A little way from the tents, Rebekah, with child at last after nearly twenty years of marriage, kneels troubled with her hands on her body, enquiring of the LORD why the children struggle within her. Radiant light shines down on her from the sky as the LORD answers that two nations are in her womb, and the elder shall serve the younger.

column8: Exactly one grown person: Rebekah, with her two newborn twin boys. No one else: no midwives and no other children.
column9: Inside a tent, seen through its open front, Rebekah rests on her bed, weary and glad, with her newborn twin sons beside her: the first red all over, covered with hair like a hairy garment, and the second holding his brother's heel in his tiny hand. Soft light falls across the mother and her sons.

column8: Exactly four people: Esau, Isaac, Jacob and Rebekah. The twins are grown men. No servants or children.
column9: Among the tents, Esau, a cunning hunter and a man of the field, comes in carrying venison he has taken, and Isaac goes out gladly to meet him, for he loves to eat of his venison. Nearby Jacob, a plain man dwelling in tents, sits at a tent door, and Rebekah, now an older woman, stands beside him with a fond hand on his shoulder.

column8: Exactly two people: Jacob and Esau, both grown men. One pot of red lentil pottage, and bread.
column9: Outside the tents, Jacob has boiled a pot of red pottage of lentils over a small fire. Esau, come in from the field and faint with hunger, raises his hand and swears to sell Jacob his birthright, while Jacob holds bread and a bowl of the red pottage, ready to give them to him.

column8: Exactly one person: Isaac. God is only radiant light, no figure or face. No stars in the sky.
column9: In a dry land struck by famine near Gerar, the ground parched and the grass withered, Isaac kneels in awe as the LORD appears to him as radiant light from the sky. The LORD tells him not to go down into Egypt but to sojourn in this land, and promises to bless him and to multiply his seed.

column8: Exactly three people: Abimelech, Isaac and Rebekah. The window is low, near the ground. Isaac and Rebekah only laugh together, his arm around her.
column9: In Gerar, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looks out through a low window of his house and sees, in the open ground beyond, Isaac sporting with Rebekah, the two laughing together with his arm around her, plainly husband and wife, though Isaac has said she is his sister. Rebekah is still fair to look upon, though no longer young.

column8: Exactly two people: Abimelech and Isaac. No guards, heralds or crowd.
column9: Before his house in Gerar, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, faces Isaac and rebukes him sternly for saying that Rebekah was his sister, when one of the people might have taken his wife. Isaac stands before the king with his head lowered, answering that he feared he would die for her.

column8: No beams or rays of light from the sky. Only a few Philistines, watching from the edge of the fields.
column9: In the land of Gerar, Isaac stands among his fields of ripe grain, which have yielded a hundredfold in the same year he sowed them, while his many servants reap the heavy harvest. Beyond the fields graze his great flocks and herds, and a few Philistine men watch from the edge of the fields, envious of him.

column8: No one digging or filling the wells; they were stopped earlier. Only Abimelech, Isaac and Isaac's servants with his flocks and herds.
column9: Beside an old well of Abraham's that the Philistines have stopped and filled with earth, Abimelech tells Isaac to go from them, for he has become much mightier than they. Isaac turns calmly to depart toward the valley of Gerar, and behind him his servants gather his flocks and herds for the journey.

column8: The herdsmen strive with words and gestures only; no blows and no weapons. Fresh water springs up in the new well.
column9: In the valley of Gerar, Isaac's servants have dug and found a well of springing water, but the herdsmen of Gerar crowd in, claiming that the water is theirs. Isaac's herdsmen stand their ground, and Isaac stands among them, troubled, beside the well he names Esek.

column8: No herdsmen of Gerar and no quarrel. Only Isaac, his household and servants, and his flocks.
column9: Having left behind a second well that the herdsmen of Gerar strove for, Isaac has moved on, and his servants have dug another well in open country, for which no one strives. Isaac stands beside it with his hands raised in thanks that the LORD has made room for them, while his tents are pitched and his flocks spread out freely around him.

column8: Exactly one person: Isaac. Night. God is only radiant light, no figure or face. No altar, servants or lanterns yet.
column9: At Beer-sheba, on the night he comes there, Isaac kneels on the open ground as the LORD appears to him as radiant light from the dark sky. The LORD tells him that he is the God of Abraham his father, that Isaac need not fear and that he will bless him, and the light falls on Isaac and the plain around him.

column8: Exactly four people: Isaac, Abimelech, Ahuzzath and Phichol. No soldiers, escort or servants.
column9: At Beer-sheba, Abimelech comes to Isaac from Gerar with Ahuzzath, one of his friends, and Phichol, the chief captain of his army. Isaac stands wary before his tent, asking why they have come when they hate him, and Abimelech opens his hands peaceably, asking for an oath and a covenant between them, for the LORD is plainly with Isaac.

column8: Abimelech and the two men with him are small and far off, going away; no soldiers. Isaac's servants come from the well.
column9: In the morning at Beer-sheba, after the feast and the oath, Abimelech and the two men with him go away in peace along the road, small in the distance. Nearer, Isaac's servants come hurrying from the well they have been digging to tell Isaac that they have found water, and Isaac turns toward them, glad.

column8: Exactly five people: Esau, his two wives, Isaac and Rebekah. No kinsmen, gifts or household.
column9: At Isaac's tents at Beer-sheba, Esau, a man of forty, brings home his two wives, Judith and Bashemath, daughters of the Hittites, in Canaanite dress. Isaac and Rebekah, an older woman now, stand together before their tent and look on with heavy hearts, for the marriages are a grief of mind to them.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac, old and blind, and Esau, a grown man. No servants.
column9: In his tent, seen through its open front, Isaac (old), his eyes so dim that he cannot see, sits up on his bed and reaches out toward Esau, his elder son, who kneels before him. Isaac bids him take his quiver and his bow, go out to the field and take venison, and make him savoury meat, that he may bless him before he dies.

column8: Exactly three people: Rebekah and Jacob by the tents, and Esau small and far off, going out to hunt. Rebekah is an old woman; Jacob is a man in his prime.
column9: Beside the tents, Rebekah, grown old, speaks urgently to Jacob, telling him to fetch two good kids from the flock so that she can make savoury meat and he can take his father's blessing. Jacob spreads his smooth hands, afraid, for Esau is a hairy man. Far off, Esau goes out to the field with his bow to hunt.

column8: Exactly two people: Rebekah, an old woman, and Jacob. The goatskins are only on his hands and the back of his neck.
column9: Beside the tents, where a pot of savoury meat made from the two kids stands by the fire with bread, Rebekah, grown old, puts the hairy skins of the kids upon Jacob's hands and upon the smooth of his neck. Jacob stands dressed in his brother Esau's goodly raiment, uneasy, glancing toward his father's tent.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac, old and blind, and Jacob. The goatskins are on Jacob's hands and neck, not his arms.
column9: Inside the tent, seen through its open front, Isaac (old), blind, sits up on his bed and feels the hairy goatskins on the hands of Jacob, who kneels close before him in his brother's goodly raiment, a dish of savoury meat and bread beside him. Isaac's face is doubtful, for the voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac, old and blind, and Jacob. Inside the tent; no fields or vineyards in view.
column9: Inside the tent, seen through its open front, Isaac (old), blind, has eaten and drunk, and Jacob has come near and kissed him; now Isaac holds him close, smelling the smell of Esau's raiment on him, and blesses him with the dew of heaven, the fatness of the earth and plenty of corn and wine. Jacob kneels before him, the emptied dish and a cup of wine beside them.

column8: Exactly two people: Esau and Isaac, old and blind. No one else.
column9: Inside the tent, seen through its open front, Esau, just come in from his hunting, holds out the savoury meat he has made from his venison and says that he is Isaac's firstborn. Isaac (old), blind, sitting on his bed, trembles very exceedingly, for another has already brought him venison and received the blessing.

column8: Exactly two people: Esau and Isaac, old and blind. No servants and no storm.
column9: Inside the tent, seen through its open front, Esau kneels before Isaac (old) and cries with a great and exceeding bitter cry, weeping aloud and begging his father to bless him also. Isaac, blind and sorrowful, lifts a hand toward him as he answers, and the dish of venison stands untouched beside them.

column8: Exactly two people: Rebekah, an old woman, and Jacob. No one else, and no packed bundle yet.
column9: At the door of a tent, Rebekah, grown old, has called Jacob to her and speaks to him low and urgently, for his brother Esau means to kill him. She tells him to flee to her brother Laban in Haran and stay there a while, until his brother's anger turns away, and Jacob listens, troubled.

column8: Exactly two people: Isaac, old and blind, and Jacob, a man in his prime. No one else.
column9: Outside his tent at Beer-sheba, Isaac (old), blind and seated, reaches out and blesses Jacob, who kneels before him dressed for the journey with a staff, and charges him not to take a wife of the daughters of Canaan but to go to Padan-aram and take a wife of the daughters of Laban, his mother's brother. Beyond them a road leads away across the hills.

column8: Exactly two people: Esau and Mahalath. Her father Ishmael is not there, and no crowd or tribe watches.
column9: Among the tents of Ishmael's people in the desert, Esau, hoping to please his father, takes Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth, to be his wife besides the wives he already has. She stands veiled before him at the door of a tent, and the open desert stretches away behind them.

column8: Exactly one person: Jacob, a man in his prime, alone. The sun has already set; dusk.
column9: After the sun has set, on the way from Beer-sheba toward Haran, Jacob, alone and weary from the journey, lies down to sleep on the stony ground of a certain place, with one of its stones under his head for a pillow and his staff beside him. Bare hills fade into the dusk around him.

column8: A ladder, not a stairway, and not glowing. The angels are men in white without wings, on the lower part of the ladder. God is only radiant light above it, no figure or face.
column9: At night on the stony ground, Jacob sleeps with his head on the stone and dreams: a ladder is set up on the earth beside him, and its top reaches to heaven. Angels go up and come down on it, seen on its lower rungs, and above, where the ladder rises into the dark sky, the LORD stands as radiant light, speaking his promise.

column8: Exactly one person: Jacob. One standing stone, the one he slept on; no altar and no building.
column9: Early in the morning, at the place he names Bethel, Jacob, awed and afraid, has set up the stone he slept on as a pillar and pours oil from a small flask upon its top. He stands before it on the stony ground, vowing that if God keeps him in the way he goes, this stone shall be God's house.

column8: Exactly three flocks of sheep lying by the well, with their shepherds. One great stone over the well's mouth. Rachel only far off, coming with her father's sheep. Midday.
column9: At high day in a field near Haran, three flocks of sheep lie by a well whose mouth is covered by a great stone, and their shepherds wait beside them for all the flocks to gather. Jacob, weary from his journey, stands among the shepherds with his staff, asking them about Laban, and far off across the field Rachel comes with her father's sheep.

column8: The great stone lies rolled aside from the well's mouth. The shepherds of the other three flocks only look on. Midday light.
column9: Jacob has rolled the great stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock of Laban, which still crowds around the well. Now he greets Rachel with a kiss as his kinswoman, weeping aloud, and tells her he is Rebekah's son, while she stands surprised among her sheep, ready to run and tell her father, and the shepherds look on.

column8: Exactly two people: Laban and Jacob. No servants, neighbours or onlookers.
column9: On the way from Haran, Laban, who has come running to meet his sister's son, throws his arms around Jacob and kisses him in welcome, before bringing him to his house. The houses of Haran stand a little way off, and open fields lie around them in the afternoon light.

column8: Exactly four people: Laban, Jacob and Laban's two daughters, Leah the elder and Rachel the younger. No servants or other women.
column9: Outside Laban's house, Laban and Jacob clasp hands on their bargain: Jacob will serve Laban seven years for Rachel, the younger daughter, beautiful and well favoured, whom he loves. Rachel stands a little way off with her sheep, and Leah, the elder, tender eyed, stands quietly by the door of the house.

column8: The feast is of men, the men of the place. The only women are Leah, veiled from head to foot, and Zilpah. No musicians or dancers.
column9: In the evening, lamps burn where Laban has gathered all the men of the place to a feast. At its edge, Laban leads his daughter Leah, veiled from head to foot, to Jacob, who waits by his tent not knowing that she is Leah, and Zilpah, the maid Laban gives to Leah, follows behind her.

column8: Exactly three people: Jacob, Laban and Leah. No servants or guests.
column9: In the morning light, Jacob has come out to confront Laban, pointing back toward the tent and asking why he has beguiled him, while Leah stands in the tent doorway with her head bowed and her veil drawn back. Laban spreads his hands calmly: in his country the younger is not given before the firstborn.

column8: Exactly four people: Laban, Jacob, Rachel and Bilhah. No guests or crowd.
column9: When the bridal week is fulfilled, Laban gives Rachel his daughter to Jacob to wife, placing her hand in his before Laban's house. Rachel is in bridal dress, and behind her stands Bilhah, the handmaid Laban gives her to be her maid, while Jacob looks at Rachel with deep love.

column8: Exactly five people: Leah, her newborn son and her three other sons, all small boys. No girls and no other women.
column9: At the door of her tent near Haran, Leah sits holding her newborn son, Judah, her face lifted in praise to the LORD, while her three other sons, Reuben, Simeon and Levi, all small boys, play on the ground around her. The tents of Jacob's household stand behind her in soft light.

column8: Exactly three people: Rachel, Jacob and Bilhah. No children.
column9: Before her tent, Rachel, envious of her sister, clutches Jacob's arm and pleads with him to give her children, or else she dies. Jacob turns to her in anger, asking if he is in God's stead, and behind Rachel stands her maid Bilhah, eyes lowered, whom Rachel gives to Jacob to wife.

column8: Exactly four people: Rachel, Bilhah and Bilhah's two sons, a newborn and a little boy. No other women or children.
column9: Before her tent, Rachel sits holding Bilhah's newborn second son, Naphtali, upon her knees, her face bright with triumph, for she says she has wrestled with her sister and prevailed. Bilhah sits beside her with her first son, Dan, a little boy, close against her.

column8: Exactly four people: Leah, Zilpah and Zilpah's two sons, a newborn and a little boy. No crowd, no singing women, no other children.
column9: Before her tent, Leah holds Zilpah's newborn second son, Asher, up in her arms, laughing with joy and saying that she is happy and will be called blessed. Zilpah, Leah's maid, sits nearby with her first son, Gad, a little boy, on her lap.

column8: Exactly three people: Leah, Rachel and Reuben, a small boy. No reapers or other people in the fields.
column9: In the days of wheat harvest, at the edge of a ripe wheat field, Leah holds the mandrakes that her small son Reuben has found in the field and brought to her, the boy standing at her side. Rachel stands before Leah with her hand held out, asking her for some of her son's mandrakes.

column8: Exactly eight people: Leah, her newborn daughter Dinah and her six sons, all young boys. No other women or children.
column9: Before her tent, Leah sits holding her newborn daughter, Dinah, while her six sons gather around her: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, all young boys, the youngest still small enough to cling to her knee. Leah's face is full of thankfulness to God.

column8: Exactly one grown person: Rachel, with her newborn son. No one else.
column9: Inside her tent, seen through its open front, Rachel, weary but overjoyed, holds her newborn son, Joseph, wrapped in cloth, and lifts her face in thanks, for God has taken away her reproach. Soft light falls across the mother and her child, and the tent is quiet around them.

column8: Exactly two people: Jacob and Laban. No wives, children or servants.
column9: Before Laban's house, Jacob asks Laban to send him away to his own place and country with his wives and children, for whom he has served him. Laban spreads his hands and pleads with him to stay, for the LORD has blessed him for Jacob's sake, and behind them Laban's flocks and herds, increased to a multitude, cover the hills.

column8: Laban's sons drive off only the speckled, spotted and ringstraked goats and the brown sheep. Jacob stays with only white sheep and plain dark goats.
column9: In a wide pasture, Laban removes every speckled, spotted and ringstraked goat, every goat with white in it and every brown sheep from his flock and gives them into the hands of his sons, who drive them away toward the far hills. Jacob, staff in hand, stays behind with the rest of Laban's flocks, the white sheep and the dark goats.

column8: Exactly one person: Jacob. The rods are green poplar, hazel and chestnut, peeled in white stripes.
column9: By the watering troughs, Jacob sits peeling white strakes in green rods of poplar, hazel and chestnut, so that the white within them shows. Other peeled rods stand in the gutters of the troughs before the flocks, which come up to drink there, sheep and goats crowding along the water.

column8: Jacob's flocks are ringstraked, speckled, spotted and brown; Laban's flocks, apart from them, are white sheep and plain dark goats.
column9: Across a broad valley, Jacob's own flocks, ringstraked, speckled, spotted and brown, strong and many, graze by themselves, kept apart from Laban's feebler flocks on the far slopes. Jacob stands among them with his staff, and around him are his menservants and maidservants, his camels and his asses.
